implementation_notes: Channel(capacity = N) is the load leveller: send suspends once the buffer is full and receive suspends while it is empty - the kotlinlang docs describe it as conceptually a BlockingQueue whose blocking operations became suspending ones - so a burst is stored and the producer is paced without blocking a thread. Workers are coroutines iterating the channel; the docs warn that consumeEach cancels the channel when it returns, so fan-out to several consumers should use an explicit for loop. close() ends consumption deterministically, and produce/`Flow.buffer(capacity)` apply the same pattern to pipelines. The classic thread-plus-blocking-queue structure is only justified at a Java interop boundary or for blocking libraries.
pitfalls: Channel() without a capacity is a rendezvous channel: send suspends until a receiver is ready, which is backpressure but not a buffer - bursts are handed straight to consumers.
consumeEach cancels the channel when its block completes, so using it for fan-out stops the other consumers; iterate with a for loop instead.
A coroutine that blocks a dispatcher thread (blocking JDBC, Thread.sleep) stalls every other coroutine on that dispatcher; wrap blocking calls in withContext(Dispatchers.IO).
Failing to cancel the worker scope on shutdown leaks coroutines holding the channel open.

variants.name: ArrayBlockingQueue with Java interop consumers
variants.implementation_notes: Where the consumers are existing blocking Java code, the pragmatic realization is the JUC queue itself: ArrayBlockingQueue(capacity) with put() suspending the producer thread and take() the consumer, driven from dedicated threads or Dispatchers.IO coroutines. This is the same structure as the Java variant seen from Kotlin; it is the right choice when a library hands you threads rather than suspending functions, and the wrong one for new pure-coroutine code where a Channel is cheaper (no thread per consumer).
pitfalls: take() blocks the calling thread: on Dispatchers.Default it starves coroutines, so use Dispatchers.IO or dedicated threads.
InterruptedException from put/take must end the worker deliberately, not be swallowed.
Like every blocking queue, it stops preserving global order as soon as several consumers run.
